title: The centurion glorifies God (Luke 23:44–49)
hookLine: Indeed this was a just man, and the crowds go home beating their breasts

lines: A HAND TO THE CHEST AT MASS.
THE CAMERA TURNS TO THE CROWD.
cards: At every Mass, near the start, Catholics say the Confiteor, the I confess. At the words through my fault, the missal has the people strike their breast: a small, old gesture, a closed hand to the chest.
Where does it come from? One place it shows up is today's reading. About the sixth hour, around noon, on the day of the crucifixion, darkness comes over the whole earth until the ninth hour.
The veil of the temple is torn down the middle. Jesus cries out with a loud voice, and dies. Then Luke turns the camera away from the cross, to the people standing in front of it.

teach.b: Luke's Jesus dies with a psalm on his lips: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." It's from Psalm thirty, thirty-one in other Bibles, a prayer of trust the Church prays at Compline, its prayer before sleep.

teach.h: A SOLDIER SAYS: A JUST MAN.
teach.b: First, the centurion, the Roman officer in charge, who watched it all up close: "Now the centurion, seeing what was done, glorified God, saying: Indeed this was a just man." Matthew and Mark have him say Son of God.
Luke has a just man, innocent, righteous, and frames it as praise: the first reaction Luke reports after the death is a Roman officer glorifying God. Second, the crowds.
They came to see a spectacle, and they go home striking their breasts. No speech, just a gesture of grief and something like guilt. Third, his friends.
All his acquaintances, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, stood afar off, watching. They can't do anything. They stay.
Some see clearly and say so. Some feel it in the chest and go home changed. Some refuse to look away.

Catholic devotion names that last kind from the old hymn Stabat Mater, the mother standing. Luke doesn't name Mary here; John does. But the women who watch him die are the women who will go to the tomb.

how: Catholics hear Luke's account of the death in the Palm Sunday Passion in the year of Luke, and pray "into thy hands" from Psalm 31 each night at Compline; at Mass they strike the breast during the Confiteor.

o: just, righteous, innocent: a centurion's word
the darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour
a word for a crowd striking their breasts

games.q: at the cross — tap the pairs.
p: indeed this was a just man

s: in Luke the centurion says this was the Son of God
that's Matthew and Mark. Luke has: indeed this was a just man.
Jesus's last words in Luke come from a psalm
"Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit," from Psalm 31 (30 in the Douay).
Luke names Mary at the foot of the cross
John names her. Luke says the women who followed him from Galilee stood afar off.

games.q: you're the Roman officer in charge of the execution. you've seen it all, the darkness, the last cry. what do you say?
o: nothing; it's just another day's work.
games.why: he glorified God, saying: indeed this was a just man. the first response Luke reports to the death is praise, from the soldier in charge.

practice: If there's a crucifix near you, look at it; if not, picture one, or simply that hill in the afternoon dark.
Don't try to feel anything in particular; just stay, the way the women stayed, afar off and watching, and come back to the picture when your mind wanders.
If you pray, say his last line from the psalm, into thy hands; if you don't, just keep your attention there.

wordCard.voice: Dikaios. The Greek word for just, righteous, innocent: what the centurion called Jesus at the cross when he glorified God. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: just, righteous, innocent, what the centurion calls Jesus in Luke 23:47.

carryVoice: Your line: a just man. A Roman soldier's words, said as praise. That's day four hundred eighty-six.
